deep.reconstruction:
Purpose: a discrete (finite-sum) derivation of the Fourier integral theorem. The finite version is also an exact aliasing (Poisson-type summation) identity. The derivation is set up on a lattice whose spacing goes to zero as a tends to infinity. The paper's verso was reused for a receipt dated Hannover, 4 Oct 1825, so the note is probably from c.1825 or later.

Setup. Let a be a positive integer and b an integer. Put λ = λ' = sqrt(2π/a), so that λλ' = 2π/a. The index p runs over all integers. The index q runs over 0, 1, ..., a-1 (a marginal note suggests a symmetric range of about -(a-1)/2 ... (a-1)/2). Let f(t) be a function vanishing at t = ±∞.

Step 1 (definition). Gauss sets
 aΩ = Σ_p Σ_q f(λp) · exp(2πi(p-b)q/a).
[Mine: Σ_{q=0}^{a-1} exp(2πi m q/a) equals a if a divides m and 0 otherwise.] Hence
 Ω = Σ_{p≡b (mod a)} f(λp) = Σ_k f(λ(b+ka)).

Step 2, equation (1). Put T = λb and U = λa = sqrt(2πa) = 2π/λ'. Then
 Ω = Σ_{k∈Z} f(T + kU).
This is the periodization of f with period U.

Step 3. Since 2π/a = λλ', the exponent can be rewritten:
 aΩ = Σ_p Σ_q f(λp) · exp(iλλ'pq - iλλ'bq).

Step 4, equation (2). Define, for fixed q,
 F(λ'q) = Σ_p λ f(λp) · exp(iλλ'pq).
This is a Riemann sum for ∫ f(t) e^{itu} dt at u = λ'q.

Step 5. Multiplying by λ gives
 aλΩ = Σ_q F(λ'q) · exp(-iλλ'bq) = Σ_q F(λ'q) · exp(-iTλ'q).

Step 6, equation (3). [Mine: 1/(aλ) = 1/sqrt(2πa) = λ'/(2π).] Therefore
 Ω = (1/2π) · λ' · Σ_q F(λ'q) · exp(-iTλ'q).
This is a Riemann sum with step λ' in the variable u.
For every finite a, (1) = (3) is an exact identity: discrete Fourier inversion applied to the aliased sequence.

Step 7 (limit, begun at the foot of the page). Let a → ∞ with λp = t and λ'q = u. Then λ, λ' → 0 and U = sqrt(2πa) → ∞, and the following hold [mine, completing the evident intent].
- With T fixed, (1) gives Ω → f(T).
- F(u) → ∫_{-∞}^{∞} f(t) e^{itu} dt.
- F(λ'q)e^{-iTλ'q} is periodic in q with period a. So the q-range can be taken symmetric, and (3) → (1/2π) ∫_{-∞}^{∞} F(u) e^{-iTu} du.
The result is the Fourier integral theorem:
 f(T) = (1/2π) ∫ du e^{-iTu} ∫ dt f(t) e^{itu}.
The next page indeed begins with ∫ e^{-nti} f(t) dt and its cos/sin form.
errors: The marginal range '-½(a-1) ... +½(a+1)' is asymmetric and has a+1 terms; presumably a slip for -½(a-1) ... +½(a-1) (a odd), i.e. a symmetric choice of residues for q.
In the a → ∞ limit with q kept in 0..a-1 literally, u = λ'q would cover only [0, ∞). The limit needs the periodicity of the summand in q (period a) to shift to a symmetric range; this is not stated.

The hypothesis 'f vanishes at ±∞' is insufficient. Absolute convergence of the lattice sums, legitimacy of interchanging Σ_p and Σ_q, and convergence of the Riemann sums all need decay/integrability of f. The limit passage is heuristic, as was standard for the time.

Minor written slips corrected on the page itself: 'a a Ω' corrected to 'aλΩ'; an extra struck 'setzt'; struck 'λq = u' corrected to 'λ'q = u'. The algebra in (1)-(3) is otherwise correct, including the constant λ'/(2π) = 1/(aλ).

results.what: Character-sum orthogonality Σ_{q=0}^{a-1} e^{2πi(p-b)q/a} = a·[p≡b mod a], used to extract the residue class b mod a from a lattice sum.
results.modern_name: Orthogonality of additive characters / discrete Fourier transform inversion

results.what: Exact finite identity: Σ_k f(T+kU) = (λ'/2π) Σ_q F(λ'q) e^{-iTλ'q}, with F(λ'q) = Σ_p λ f(λp) e^{iλλ'pq}, step sizes λ = λ' = sqrt(2π/a), λλ' = 2π/a.
results.modern_name: Discrete Poisson summation / aliasing formula for the DFT on a symmetric (λ = λ' = sqrt(2π/N)) grid
results.usually_credited_to: Poisson (1823) for continuous Poisson summation; discrete aliasing relations are 20th-century numerical-analysis folklore

results.what: Derivation of the Fourier integral theorem f(T) = (1/2π)∫e^{-iTu}∫f(t)e^{itu}dt du as the a → ∞ limit of the finite DFT identity.
results.modern_name: Fourier integral (inversion) theorem, derived as limit of the discrete Fourier transform

deep.surprise_reason: The Fourier integral theorem itself was known by 1825 (Fourier, Cauchy, Poisson), and Gauss's mastery of the DFT (1805) is well known. The notable feature is the method. It is a clean, exact finite DFT/aliasing identity on a symmetric grid with λ = λ' = sqrt(2π/a), passed to the limit to obtain Fourier inversion. That is a modern-looking derivation linking Gauss's discrete trigonometric interpolation with the continuous transform. It is a notable unpublished detail, but not a priority-changing result.

checkable.asserts: Orthogonality: the sum over q of exp(2πi m q/a) is a if a | m, else 0.
U = λa equals 2π/λ' when λ = λ' = sqrt(2π/a) (expect 0).

checkable.sympy: a=5; b=2; lam=sqrt(2*pi/a); f=lambda t: exp(-t**2); T=lam*b; F=lambda u: sum(lam*f(lam*p)*exp(I*lam*p*u) for p in range(-40,41)); lhs=sum(f(lam*(b+k*a)) for k in range(-10,11)); rhs=lam/(2*pi)*sum(F(lam*q)*exp(-I*T*lam*q) for q in range(a)); N(lhs-rhs)
checkable.asserts: The exact finite identity (1) = (3) for a Gaussian f (expect ≈ 0, up to truncation).
The limiting Fourier inversion formula reached at the foot of the page, checked for f = exp(-t^2) (expect 0).
